Senses.Explanation: Literally, transmit the lamp. The expression uses one lamp lighting the next for continuation from teacher to successor. Records pair it with continuing the flame, say that lamp follows lamp and ancestor transmits to ancestor, and ask what is being continued. The preface to the Jingde Record explicitly calls it 'the comparison of transmitting the lamp.' A later preface gives its own intensified definition: 'transmitting the lamp is transmitting this hot flame.' That hot-flame equation belongs to that preface's five-lamps discussion and is not imposed on every occurrence.
Senses.Note: Across both senses the headword occurs 982 times in 210 allowlisted texts. The succession formula 'lamp after lamp continues' occurs 71 times in 58 texts; 'continue the flame and transmit the lamp' occurs twice in two texts.

Senses.PreferredTarget: book or record title: Transmission of the Lamp
Senses.Explanation: As a title element and shorthand, the compound names the historical lamp-record genre. The headword plus 'record' occurs 382 times in 61 allowlisted texts. The Jingde preface says that a thirty-volume work covering fifty-two generations and 1,701 people was titled the Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp. The Continued Record of the Transmission of the Lamp uses the same compound in its title. A later discourse enumerates five lamp works by shorthand: Transmission Lamp, Broad Lamp, Universal Lamp, Continued Lamp, and Linked Lamp.
Senses.Note: This bibliographic sense is distinguished because occurrences often refer to a named book or family of records rather than the act of succession. The literal lamp image remains visible in the titles.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'transmit the robe.' The compound occurs 430 times in 162 allowed texts. In lineage histories it names a physical handover associated with succession. The fullest direct account is Hongren's answer after giving Huineng the inherited robe. He says, 'When Bodhidharma first arrived, people did not yet trust; therefore the robe was transmitted to make clear that the teaching had been obtained. Now confidence is mature, the robe has become a source of contention; it stops with you and will not be transmitted again' (昔達磨初至，人未知信，故傳衣以明得法。今信心已熟，衣乃爭端，止於汝身，不復傳也). This account both states the robe's recorded evidentiary function and the reason given for ending its transmission. Other histories narrate that the time to transmit the robe arrived, that Hongren gave Huineng the robe and told him to guard what was entrusted, and that the transfer occurred secretly at night. Later records use the event as chronology, lineage claim, question, and criticism: one asks what is entrusted after Caoxi because 'from this point the robe and bowl were not transmitted' (自此不傳衣鉢), while Fuyan Baozong's address lists 'Huineng transmitting the robe through six generations, seeking that small advantage' (盧公六代傳衣，圖他小利). The collocation 'transmit the robe and entrust the teaching' (傳衣付法) occurs 26 times in 22 texts, 'transmit robe and bowl' (傳衣鉢) 31 times in 26, and 'not transmit the robe' (不傳衣) 16 times in 15.
Senses.Note: The primary sense is the lineage robe handover recorded across lamp histories, discourse records, and later comments. The entry does not treat possession of the robe as proof beyond Hongren's own quoted explanation, and it preserves the corpus's criticism and discontinuation language. Repetitions of the Hongren-Huineng event are parallel witnesses to one reported event, not separate events.

Senses.Explanation: In one seventeenth-century record, the same compound occurs seven times after addresses connected with receiving precepts. The recurring stage direction is 'having handed out the robes' (傳衣竟), followed by 'he descended from the seat' (下座) or the next address. One occurrence says that those receiving the complete set came forward and, after the robes had been handed out, the speaker recited a further statement. Here the verb names distribution during the recorded ceremony, not the lineage transfer from Hongren to Huineng.
Senses.Note: All seven exact hits for this use are in the Recorded Sayings of Konggu Daocheng; no independent headword-bearing witness was found. The broader phrase 'bestow a robe' (授衣) occurs across the corpus, but it is a different headword and does not raise this sense above provisional.
